This was the first launch test of this missile. It was originally scheduled to be launched in 1994, but was cancelled. This missile was also cancelled after this test.
While the distance of the test was not recorded, we know that the Hatf-1 has a range of at least 80 km, and is disputed to be capable of reaching 100 km
At this time, Indian officials stated that if the Agni was further developed it would be as a conventional weapons delivery system and did not want to be viewed as a nuclear weapons power.

Indian PM stated that it would only be used as a conventional weapons system but experts believe that it is too close in design to the Soviet SCUD missile and lacks the accuracy to deliver surgical strikes -- better suited for nuclear or chemical warheads.
The exact date of this test is not clear. The date is entered as January 1 but the test could have occurred on any day in 1992.

This is an improved version of the Hatf-1 known as the Hatf-1A. It is disputed whether this variant was introduced in 1992 or 1995. Different sources have conflicting information on this. This variant is known to have a range of 100km with greater accuracy
ISRO lists this launch as the third successful developmental launch of the ASLV
First launch of the Prithvi-II
First test fire of Prithvi-II - ability to strike most important cities and military targets in Pakistan
India stated that it would resist international efforts to contain its success in strategic areas

While Pakistan has carried out missile tests as far back as 1962, this is the first test that was either not a sounding rocket or not lacking the required range and payload requirements to meet the criteria for this data set. The Ghauri Missile is a copy of North Korea's Nodong-1 Missile, according to the Federation of American Scientists. The missile was also handled originally by A.Q. Khan Research Labratories, but was handed over to the Pakistani Army in 2003.

This test launch was claimed as "highly successful" by Pakistani military.The development of the Shaheen was particularly important because the missile's range extended all of India, so even critical cities such as New Delhi would be hit. The testing of these missiles also made China more vulnerable. China began pushing harder for peaceful dialogue between Pakistan and India once these missiles (and India's Agni) were developed.
Pakistan is believed to have created the Ghauri-II in response to this missile program.

This was the first lanch of the Ghauri-2. The missile was launched in response to India's missile test of the Agni-2 IRBM which was launched on 11-Apr-99.There was suspicion, especially from the U.S., that the Ghauri-2 was really just another testing of the Ghauri-1. This test made it clear that Pakistan desired to keep up with India.
This test was done in response to India's test of the Agni-2 missile. Also, this missile was meant to counter the Prithvi Missile (India's missile)
Fourth successive successful test flight of the PSLV
This is an improved version of the Hatf-1A, known as the 1B. It has the same capabilities as its predecessor.
Flew for four seconds before breaking apart

This missile development was in direct response to India's Agni-3 missile. It is uncear if this was a test of the Ghauri-3 or actually a Ghauri-2 test. Much of the program remains secret and it was eventually shut down.
Pakistan and Japan were notified in advance in accordance with an agreement signed in Lahore in 1999
First Indian GSLV launch; the first launch was aborted one second before liftoff on March 28, 2001
First developmental test flight of the BrahMos cruise missile
India began developing satellite imaging capabilities in response to Pakistan entering the disputed Kashmir region in 1999 ; second time India has launched 3 satellites at once successfully.
Launched by the airforce. The Prithvi-I is already in the service of the army

The decision to test fell during a time of increased tension between India and Pakistan - Pakistan reported that Indian forces were amassed all along the border. Indian officials reported that the test was to demonstrate their nuclear capabilities to deter a Pakistani attack.
Developmental test flight
This missile program as well as the development of the Shaheen missile were primarily concerned with reaching the eastern region of India.
First Launch of the Ghaznavi. Missile is believed to be a Pakistani-assembled version of the Chinese M-11 missile

During these tests, India continued to claim that they were unphased. This test also occurred two days before Pakistan's parliamentary elections as well as two days before India holding their last roud of disputed state poll in Kashmir.
Little information is available about this test, it may not have happened
Test was carried out with a dummy warhead

Developmental test flight. Location of test somewhat uncertain, media reports state test took place off coast of India in Bay of Bengal. Other Indian missile tests in Bay of Bengal took place in the Integrated Test Range, exact location within the range is unclear.

Pakistan is reported to have conducted this test only  a few hours after India conducted a test of its Prithvi SRBM. Pakistan said the test did not relate to India's test. Nobody really believes that though.
Shortly after reports of this launch, Pakistan reported a successful launch of their Abdali missile
This may have been the Prithvi-II. Sources are divided on the type of missile tested.
This missile is similar to the Abdali program and both resemble the Chinese missile, the M-11. Pakistan claimed that this missile was not in response to India, but to their own defense needs.

There is disagreement over some details of this test. Some sources list the test as occurring in Sonmiani instead and as a Shaheen 3. Also, during the beginning of 2004, this is when Pakistan and India began initial peace talks. The test also came 8 days before Secretary of State, Colin Powell went to Pakistan (to discuss nuclear concerns, in part). This was also the first test of a 2-stage missile.
Analysts stated that the successful launch of this solid-fuel missile guarantees India's credible nuclear deterrence

A Pakistani defense official claimed that India was warned prior to this test. Pakistan also said that the test was not in response to India. Apparently the intention of the test was to placate any domestic fears that Pakistan was scaling down its suclear program.
Prithvi-3 successfully launched for first time

India was also given advanced notice of this missile test. This test, in particular, was done due to the clear weahter in order for scientists to track the flight path of this missile. Many outisders such as the U.S. believed that the test migth have been in response to growing tentions on the Korean Peninsula, keeping in mind the tie between North Korea and Pakistan.

First time the Brahmos was launched from land to hit a land-based target. Media reports identify the test location as "Rajasthan", this is likely the Pokhran Test Range which is located in the province.
Condoleezza Rice visited Pakistan to encourage its peace talks with India. Two days afterwards, Pakistan carried out this test.
First launch from new second PSLV launch pad at Sriharikota

This missile was developed in response to India acquiring the Patriot Missile. This was the missile's first launch. In response to India and the Patriot missiles, the Babur was also developed to prevent radar recognition and to permeate the enemy's air defense. Also, this missile is comparable to India's Nirbhay Cruise Missile.
This missile was fired a day after the U.S. and Pakistan endered a two day dialogue, but failed when the Bush Admin. failed to offer a civil nuclear energy deal to Islamabad.

Few reports exist about this test, it may not have happened or involved a different, much smaller missile system. The exact date of the test is also unknown, the only available report records it as June 2006.
Mixed reports indicating that it failed at some point in the launch
This test followed domestic criticism a day after peace talks with India.
India claims it as a "missile defense milesone"

The military claimed this test was meant to confirm the design parameters for this missile.
This was the first testing of the Ra'ad Missile. It is more difficult to detect, so this could potentially be seen as Pakistan reacting to India's anti- ballistic defense system.

This missile test was a part of a routine military training exercise. The Chief of Army Staff, Parvez Kiyani, responded to international concerns about these weapons falling into the wrong hands after this missile test. He supported the safeguards of the missile program claiming that it was very safe.
India's first submerged launch of a ballistic missile. Test is believed to have taken place off the coast of Visakhapatnam. The missile itself was fired from a submerged pontoon.
SBCM hit a land target for the first time

This test lauch was in reaction to a test of an  India developed missile capable of striking targets deep inside China. Pakistani military also claimes that this missile has a low probability of detection due to stealth design as well as the materials used in its construction. Also, this test came a day after India successfully launched the Agni-3.
Launched the first Indian lunar probe which impacted with the moon at 15:01 GMT and scanned for lunar polar ice.

Pakistan has never acknowledged this test. The report comes from a NYT article in which the Obama admin accussed Pakistan of illegally modifying the Harpoon missiles sold to Pakistan in the 1980s to add a land attack mode. It's unclear what missile was tested, where the test took place, or what the outcome was based on available information. This is currently recorded as a Babur test because a test on May 6 was said to be of a missile similar to this test and that was a Babur test.

The announcement of this launch wasnlt made until May 9th, 2009, due to "political reasons". At the time, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari was visiting the United States. The US later accused Pakistan of making this missile by modifying US-made harpoon missiles which were sold to Pakistan in the 1980s.
This launched 7 payloads (with differing apogees) including 2 civilian communication satellites, 3 technology satellites, 1 science satellite, and 1 surveillance satellite.
Twin trial of two Prithvi-II, India referred to this as a "user trial", suggesting it was an operational exercise of the system intended to partially simulate wartime conditions.
Twin trial of two Prithvi-II

Fourth Agni-3 test

The test was carried out from an underwater barge meant to simulate a submarine launch of the missile. The exact date of the test is not clear. Initially, the Shaurya was believed to be a new ballistic missile, following the success of this test, the Indian government revelaed it was a hypersonic cruise missile. Following the test, V K Saraswat, the DRDO chief and Scientific Advisor to the Defence Minister, stated at a 2010 defense exposition, “We have designed the Shaurya so that it can be launched from under water as easily as from land. The gas-filled canister that houses the missile fits easily into a submarine. The underwater leg of the nuclear triad needs to be totally reliable and needs a state-of-the-art missile.” Unlike the first and third test of this system, media reports on the second test have been extremely limited.
Launched as part of a test of India's missile defense system, this missile reportedly deviated from its intended course. The test was aborted midway through the test.

This missile program is believed to have been terminated in 2007, but aproximately 30-50 missiles are thought to remain in the stockpile.

This test of two missiles was a part of a training exercise carried out by Pakistan's strategic command. Following the test, Pakistan demanded it be admitted into the Nuclear Suppliers Group as a legitimate nuclear power.

This was the first launch of the Shaheen 1A. This test also came a week after a successful test of a long- range missile from India (the Agni-5). This can be interpreted as another instance where Pakistan misinterpreted India's missile test, as India claimed the missile test was a response to China not Pakistan. Information on the missile's range was extremely scattered, ranging from 1500 km to 3000 km.

served as an interceptor for the prithvi. This test is believed to have failed for unknown reasons. Little information on this test is available in the public sphere.
Remnants from this missile fell into Dadu in the Sind Province suggesting the test was a failure. Pakistan denies the claim and says the missile test was a complete success.

Following this test, Pakistan stated it was not worried about the test of this missile because it understood that it would not be cost effective to fire at shorter ranges and that it also believed this missile was intended for China. Pakistan indicated that it would continue developing its shorter-range missiles
First Indian mission to Mars

There appear to be conflicting reports about the date of the this test. Several sources state or suggest Pakistan carried out a successful four missile salvo test of the Nasr, after which the rocket officially entered service. However, one source claims the test occurred on October 5, 2013 while a press release from the Pakistani Army suggests it was conducted on November 5, 2013 instead. It is quite possible Pakistan waited a month before publicly announcing the test or that the October 5 report was made in error. It is also possible there were two distinct sets of tests in October and November, however, we were not able to locate any additional information supporting an October 5 test claim.
second dedicated navigation satellite

Training exercise

third dedicated navigation satellite

Reportedly this was a test of an enhanced version of the missile, able to hit a target withou the aid from GPS. There are still comparisons between the Babur and and Nirbhay; apparently India did not have any matching capabilites before this test of the Babur cruise missile.

India initially expressed skepticism about this test prompting Pakistan to carry out an additional test. This was the first launch of a Pakistani SLCM, marking the completion of Pakistan's nuclear triad. The test was likely carried out in response to India's Agni V.

Some India news reports initially claimed this was a successful test. However, others disputed this claim and stated it failed. Satellite images, obtained recently by a group of independent researchers at Monterey, confirmed that the test failed.

It's unclear if more than one Nasr missile was fired, past tests have involved firing a volley of Nasr missiles. Pakistan claimed the test was of an upgraded version of the Nasr missile which increased its range from 60km to 70km.
India's first indigenously designed long-range cruise missile

The cruise missile was launched from an IAF su-30MKI aircraft. Location of test somewhat uncertain, media reports state test took place off coast of India in Bay of Bengal. The missile is claimed to have athe ability to strike land and sea-based targets. Pakistan claims it carries a new terrain mapping navigation system which allows it to strike targets even without GPS.

Media reports state that the test was carried out about 10 km off the coast of Visakhapatnam. Despite three missile launches, there were no reports about the tests until a week later on August 19 when local media picked up the story. Media reports state that the Arihant, the submarine the test was carried out on, had previously carried out a K-15 test in November 2015. Researchers have been unable to confirm this was an actual flight test and not a test of a dummy missile as some reports have suggested.
The test was noteable as a user trial of the missile. In addition, the test was only the second reported night trial of the Agni-1, the first being held on April 12, 2014.
This test involved a full, four missile salvo.

The exact date of the launch is not clear. Satellite images show a missile on a launch pad at the test location and Pakistan had announced plans to conduct a missile test. However, an announcement of a successful test did not follow which strongly suggests the test failed. Unfortunately there is not clear evidence to suggest the test even took place, it may have been scrubbed at the last minute and rescheduled for a later date.
This launch occurred within a week of the test prior to it, and was said to test the extreme in-flight and end-flight maneuverability
Believed to be a failed ASAT test. This test is recorded as a failure given that it did not intercept the satellite. India maintains this was an ABM test but without an intercept target.
India's first successful ASAT test. The missile impacted the target. A test a few months prior appears to have failed to intercept the target.
Pakistan is believed to have tested an unknown sea launched land attack cruise missile. It is unknown what kind of missile it was however. The test appears to have been successful.
India's mission to send a rover to the moon. The rocket successfully launched after a week long technical delay. The rover is expected to reach lunar orbit in September 2019.

India conducted two Brahmos tests over a two day period. The details are not available (1 of 2). In late November it was disclosed that the missiles struck their target on Trak Island in the Car Nicobar Islands.
